title: Energy Resources and Power Generation

facts.printed_claim: Resources are environmental materials useful for satisfying human needs and supporting cultural, economic and political change.
Soil, water, air, minerals, rivers, forests and energy resources are examples of resources.
Resources can be classified by origin into biotic and abiotic resources.
Biotic resources originate from living components of the biosphere; humans, flora, fauna and animal products are examples.
Abiotic resources are non-living; rocks, minerals, air, water, solar energy and soil are printed examples.
By exhaustibility, resources are classified as renewable and non-renewable.
Renewable resources can be replenished through physical, chemical or mechanical processes; printed examples are solar, wind, water, forests and wildlife.
Non-renewable resources are depleted by use and form over millions of years; minerals and fossil fuels are examples.
Metals can be recycled, whereas fossil fuels cannot be recycled after combustion.
The printed December 2025 table gives total installed electricity capacity as 476 GW.
The printed December 2025 table gives thermal capacity as 240 GW or 50.5%.
The printed December 2025 table gives non-fossil capacity as 236 GW or 49.5%.
Within the printed total, renewable capacity is 227 GW and nuclear capacity is 8.8 GW.
The printed renewable breakup is solar 110 GW, wind 51 GW, hydro 48 GW and biomass 18 GW.
The book describes conventional energy as long-used sources and lists hydel, coal, petroleum, natural gas, thermal power and nuclear power.
The book describes non-conventional sources as more recently developed or promoted sources.
Printed renewable non-conventional examples include solar, wind, biogas, biomass, biodiesel, bioethanol, small hydro and bagasse cogeneration.
Printed modern-energy examples include hydrogen, geothermal, battery-operated vehicles, ocean thermal-gradient energy, tidal power, ocean-current energy, fuel gas, coal-bed methane and gas hydrates.
The Government of India established the Commission for Additional Sources of Energy (CASE) in 1981.
Thermal electricity is produced using coal, petroleum, diesel or natural gas as fuel.
Thermal power has the largest share in India's electricity generation in the printed discussion.
NTPC was established in 1975 for thermal-power development.
A small hydropower project is printed as one with capacity up to 25 MW.
India's printed small-hydro potential is about 25,000 MW, concentrated especially in Himalayan and Western Ghats regions.
Solar photovoltaic cells convert sunlight directly into electricity.
The book identifies a 100 kW solar project at Kalyanpur village in Aligarh district, Uttar Pradesh, as an early Indian project.
The book says solar-energy use is led by China, with the United States in third place.
The book links PM-KUSUM with replacing diesel-based irrigation by solar pumps and cites a 35-lakh pump benefit figure.
Wind turbines convert the kinetic energy of moving air into electricity.
The book identifies Veraval, Gujarat, in 1985 as India's first wind-power plant.
The book gives Muppandal, Tamil Nadu, as the largest wind plant with 1,500 MW.
The printed AP wind locations are Tirumala and Anantapur.
The book states India ranks fourth in wind power after China, the United States and Germany.
Biogas can be produced from plant residues, animal wastes, dung, municipal wastes and sewage; it is also called gobar gas, swamp gas or landfill gas in different contexts.
The printed principal biogas composition is methane 60-70% and carbon dioxide 30-40%.
The book says government subsidies support rural biogas-plant construction.
The book identifies Jabalpur as the site of India's first biogas centre.
The book reports about 50,000 biogas plants by 2018.
The book links the Kisan Prakriya project at Murganathad with biogas production.
The book mentions a 1983 Prana Mitra award for promoting smokeless chulhas in rural areas.
The book states Denmark produces the highest percentage of energy from biogas.
The printed June 2021 estimate of Indian wave-energy potential is 10,170 MW, with Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh and Karnataka named as higher-potential states.
Biodiesel is made through transesterification of plant oils or animal fats using alcohol and a catalyst.
Printed biodiesel feedstocks include canola, soybean, palm, rapeseed and oils from plants such as Jatropha.
B100 denotes pure biodiesel; B20 denotes a blend of 20% biodiesel and 80% petroleum diesel.
Bioethanol is produced by fermenting glucose derived from crops or organic feedstocks and is blended with petrol to reduce fossil-fuel use.
The book states India achieved 10% ethanol blending in 2022 and advanced the 20% target from 2030 to 2025-26.
The book cites projected foreign-exchange savings of ₹90,000 crore from reaching the 20% ethanol target.
The Central Government declared 2022-23 as Ethanol Supply Year (ESY) in the printed text.
Hydrogen fuel cells generate electricity through an electrochemical reaction of hydrogen and oxygen.
The book places the announcement of the National Hydrogen Energy Mission in the 2021-22 Union Budget.
Wave energy uses sea-wave motion; the book mentions Vizhinjam near Thiruvananthapuram and a Mus Point location in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
Tidal energy exploits periodic sea-level changes caused by tides; printed locations include Gulf of Kachchh, Gulf of Khambhat, Sundarbans and Durgaduani Creek.
Ocean thermal-gradient energy uses the temperature difference between warm surface water and cold deep water.
The book names Tuticorin, Andaman-Nicobar and Kulashekarapatnam as possible ocean-thermal-gradient locations.
Geothermal energy uses heat from Earth's interior, commonly associated with hot springs or geysers.
Printed geothermal locations include Manikaran, Puga, Chumathang, Surajkund, Tapovan, Tattapani, Cambay, Bakreshwar and Jalgaon.
The book says a 20 kW geothermal plant at Manuguru in Bhadradri Kothagudem district was approved in June 2021 and uses an Organic Rankine Cycle.

Electricity is treated as a subject involving both Union and State governments under India's constitutional system.
The book associates the Electricity (Supply) Act with 1948.

The book states that Madhya Pradesh ranked second after reforms were implemented.
Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Gram Jyoti Yojana (DDUGJY) is presented as a Union scheme for rural electrification.
DDUGJY provides for separation of agricultural and non-agricultural feeders in rural areas.
DDUGJY includes strengthening of rural sub-transmission and distribution infrastructure.
The book says the earlier RGGVY rural-electrification programme was subsumed/continued under DDUGJY.

The book calls Andhra Pradesh first in the country in implementation of the LED street-lighting method.
